title: Week 1 Material
notes: A modern computer includes CPUs, main memory, storage, I/O devices, and network interfaces, forming a complex system that needs coordinated control.
Chapter 1 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
An operating system is a software layer that provides a simpler model of the computer and manages hardware resources for programs.
Chapter 1 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Most systems support kernel mode and user mode; the operating system runs in kernel mode with complete hardware access.
Chapter 1 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
User-mode programs are restricted from executing privileged instructions, especially those that control the machine or perform direct I/O.
Chapter 1 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
A shell or GUI is usually a user-mode program that starts other programs and relies on the operating system for services.
Chapter 1 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Operating systems perform two core functions: providing clean abstractions and managing hardware resources among competing programs and users.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Good abstractions require defining and implementing the abstraction, then using it to solve problems without dealing with messy hardware details.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
The file abstraction hides disk hardware complexity and presents a simple interface for storing information.
Chapter 1 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
The operating system’s real customers are application programs, while end users interact through shells or graphical user interfaces.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
As a resource manager, the OS allocates CPU, memory, and I/O devices and mediates conflicts when multiple programs compete for them.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
The OS can prevent printer chaos by buffering output and printing each job in an orderly sequence rather than interleaving lines.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Time multiplexing shares a resource by letting programs take turns, such as scheduling CPU time among multiple runnable processes.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Space multiplexing shares a resource by partitioning it, such as dividing main memory so multiple programs remain resident.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
A CPU fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and executes them, using registers to store temporary values and control state.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
The program counter holds the memory address of the next instruction, allowing execution to proceed sequentially or via branches.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
The stack pointer tracks the top of the current stack in memory, supporting procedure calls, local variables, and return addresses.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
The program status word stores condition codes and control bits, including priority and mode information used by the CPU.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
During context switches, the OS must save and restore registers so each program can resume correctly after being time-multiplexed.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
CPU multithreading allows fast switching between thread states on a nanosecond timescale, reducing switching cost but not true parallelism.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Multicore chips include multiple independent CPU cores, enabling true parallel execution when the OS schedules work across cores.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Memory is organized as a hierarchy: registers, cache, main memory (RAM), and nonvolatile storage, balancing speed, cost, and capacity.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Cache is divided into cache lines; frequently used lines are kept close to the CPU to reduce average memory access time.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Main memory is the workhorse RAM that bridges fast cache and slower nonvolatile storage, holding active programs and data.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
I/O devices have a controller plus the device; controllers differ, so the OS uses device drivers to control each controller type.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Device drivers typically run in kernel mode so they can access device registers and perform privileged I/O operations safely.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Devices signal completion or events using interrupts; the OS runs an interrupt handler selected via the interrupt vector table.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
Buses connect components; a large x86 system may include PCIe, USB, SATA, memory buses, and others with different speeds.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
PCIe uses dedicated point-to-point serial connections rather than a shared bus, improving throughput and reducing contention.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 1.pdf
A system call transitions from user space to kernel space using a trap instruction, switching modes so the kernel can run.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
System call parameters are prepared and passed to a library procedure, which places a system-call number and triggers the trap.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
System calls report errors by returning a failure code and setting the global variable errno with error information.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
The fork() system call creates a duplicate process; after fork, parent and child execute separately and may use copy-on-write memory.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
The waitpid() system call lets a parent wait for a specific child or any child to terminate and retrieve the exit status.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
The execve() system call replaces a process’s core image with a new program, commonly used by shells to run user commands.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
A process is an executing program instance with its own program counter, registers, and variables managed by the OS.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Multiprogramming rapidly switches the CPU among processes to provide pseudo-parallel execution even on a single CPU.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
A process table is an array of entries storing per-process state such as registers, stack pointer, memory allocation, and file status.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
The lowest layer of a process-structured OS handles interrupts and scheduling, selecting which process runs next.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Threads allow multiple execution paths within one process, sharing the same address space and data for efficient communication.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Threads are lighter than processes and can be created or destroyed much faster, which helps highly dynamic servers.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Threads improve performance when computation overlaps with I/O, but provide little benefit if all threads are purely CPU-bound.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Processes group resources like address space and open files, while threads are the entities scheduled for execution by the CPU.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Each thread has its own stack for local variables and return addresses, creating synchronization and shared-resource design challenges.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
User-level threads use a per-process thread table in user space and avoid kernel traps, making thread operations fast.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
User-level threads can block the entire process if one thread page faults, and lack clock interrupts can allow runaway threads.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Kernel threads are tracked in a kernel thread table; creating or destroying them uses system calls and has higher overhead.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Kernel threads handle page faults efficiently by scheduling another runnable thread, but multithreaded forking and signals are harder.
Operating Systems - Week 1 Lesson 2.pdf
Type 1 hypervisors run on bare hardware and provide multiple virtual machines, while type 2 hypervisors rely on a host OS.
Chapter 1 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Containers package apps with their libraries while sharing the host operating system, unlike VMs that include full guest operating systems.

quiz.question: Which two essential functions are emphasized for an operating system in Week 1 materials?
options: Providing clean abstractions and managing hardware resources
Compiling source code and optimizing machine instructions
Encrypting files and providing internet routing
Building hardware drivers and manufacturing devices
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The materials define the OS as both an abstraction provider and a resource manager.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between kernel mode and user mode?
options: Kernel mode runs only application code, while user mode runs only device drivers
Kernel mode has full hardware access, while user mode has restricted privileges
Kernel mode cannot access memory, while user mode can
Kernel mode is slower than user mode because it uses cache
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Kernel mode permits privileged instructions and direct hardware access, unlike user mode.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the shell or GUI in Tanenbaum’s description?
options: It is always part of the kernel and runs in kernel mode
It is the lowest level of user-mode software that starts other programs
It replaces the operating system when running applications
It is a device driver responsible for I/O interrupts
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The shell/GUI is user-mode software that uses OS services to launch and manage programs.

quiz.question: A major reason operating systems provide abstractions like files is to:
options: Eliminate the need for any hardware drivers
Hide complex and awkward hardware interfaces from applications
Prevent programs from using memory
Guarantee every program runs in parallel
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Files and other abstractions simplify programming by hiding device-level complexity.

quiz.question: Time multiplexing primarily refers to:
options: Dividing memory into partitions for multiple programs
Sharing a resource by letting programs take turns using it
Storing identical copies of data in cache and RAM
Assigning different buses to different devices permanently
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Time multiplexing means turn-taking on a resource such as the CPU.

quiz.question: Which is an example of space multiplexing?
options: Round-robin CPU scheduling among processes
Spooling printer output to disk
Dividing main memory among multiple resident programs
Using interrupts to signal I/O completion
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Space multiplexing allocates different parts of a resource like memory to different programs.

quiz.question: Which CPU register holds the address of the next instruction to execute?
options: Stack pointer
Program counter
Program status word
Cache line register
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The program counter stores the memory address of the next instruction.

quiz.question: Which CPU register points to the top of the current call stack in memory?
options: Stack pointer
Program counter
PSW
I/O port register
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The stack pointer tracks the top of the current stack used for calls and returns.

quiz.question: What does the Program Status Word (PSW) contain, according to the Week 1 hardware review?
options: Only the next instruction address
Condition codes and control bits such as priority and mode
Only open file descriptors
Only cache line tags
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The PSW includes condition code bits plus control information like CPU mode and priority.

quiz.question: Why must the operating system save and restore registers during time multiplexing?
options: To prevent cache lines from being overwritten
To preserve each process’s CPU state across context switches
To increase disk storage capacity
To avoid using interrupts
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Saving/restoring registers preserves execution state so a process can resume correctly.

quiz.question: CPU multithreading, as presented in the slides, primarily:
options: Creates true parallelism on a single core
Reduces thread-switching time by keeping multiple thread states available
Eliminates the need for an operating system scheduler
Prevents any context switching
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Multithreading reduces switching overhead but does not provide true parallelism on one core.

quiz.question: Which hardware feature enables true parallel execution of threads without time slicing on one core?
options: Multithreading
Multicore processors
Program counter
Interrupt vector table
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Multiple cores are independent CPUs that can execute in parallel.

quiz.question: In the memory hierarchy, which component is typically fastest?
options: Magnetic disk/SSD
Main memory (RAM)
Cache
CPU registers
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Registers are inside the CPU and operate at CPU speed, making them the fastest layer.

quiz.question: Why do caches use cache lines (blocks) rather than caching single bytes only?
options: Because disks require 64-byte reads
Because programs exhibit locality, so nearby bytes are likely to be used soon
Because user mode forbids single-byte caching
Because interrupts only work with cache lines
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Caching blocks exploits spatial locality by fetching nearby data likely needed soon.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes an I/O device in the slides?
options: An I/O device is only the physical peripheral and has no controller
An I/O device consists of a controller plus the device itself
An I/O device is the same as main memory
I/O devices are controlled directly by user programs
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The slides describe I/O devices as having a controller and the device hardware.

quiz.question: Why are device drivers typically placed in the operating system and run in kernel mode?
options: Drivers need privileged access to device registers and I/O instructions
Drivers must be written in Java to run safely
Drivers only manage user interfaces like shells
Drivers cannot interact with interrupts
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Kernel mode allows drivers to perform privileged hardware operations safely.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the interrupt vector table?
options: Store every file name on disk
Map interrupt numbers to interrupt service routine addresses
Assign IP addresses to devices
Record cache line contents
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The interrupt vector table maps interrupts to the correct handler code in memory.

quiz.question: Which bus characteristic is highlighted for PCIe in the Week 1 slides?
options: Shared parallel bus with one device at a time
Dedicated point-to-point serial connections
Only usable for keyboards
Used exclusively for CPU registers
quiz.explanation: Correct because: PCIe is described as a dedicated point-to-point serial interconnect.

quiz.question: What triggers the user-to-kernel transition for a system call?
options: A cache miss
A trap instruction
A printer spool file
A disk seek
quiz.explanation: Correct because: System calls use a trap instruction to switch into kernel mode.

quiz.question: In the system call workflow described in Week 1 Lesson 2, which happens first?
options: Kernel dispatches to the system-call handler
Trap instruction executes and switches modes
Parameters are prepared and a library procedure is called
Control returns to the user program
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Parameters are prepared and passed to a library procedure before the trap instruction.

quiz.question: How is error information commonly exposed to user programs after a system call fails (as in the slides)?
options: The OS prints a message to the screen automatically
The failing system call sets a global variable named errno
The system reboots to prevent corruption
The CPU disables user mode permanently
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The slides state errors are indicated and detailed in the global variable errno.

quiz.question: What does fork() do in POSIX-style process management?
options: Replaces the current process image with a new program
Creates a child process identical to the parent at the moment of creation
Waits for a child process to terminate
Terminates the process immediately
quiz.explanation: Correct because: fork duplicates the calling process, creating a parent and child that then execute separately.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of waitpid()?
options: Create a new process
Wait for a child process to terminate and collect its status
Replace the program being executed
Switch a user thread without kernel involvement
quiz.explanation: Correct because: waitpid blocks until a child exits and returns exit status details.

quiz.question: What does execve() do in the shell example?
options: Duplicates the parent process
Replaces the process core image with the program specified
Blocks until all children terminate
Moves the file pointer within a file
quiz.explanation: Correct because: execve replaces the current process image with a new program to run the command.

quiz.question: Which best matches the process model described in Week 1 Lesson 2?
options: Runnable software is organized into sequential processes, each an executing program instance
All programs share one set of registers and one program counter
Only kernel threads exist; processes are obsolete
Processes are files stored on disk
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The slides describe processes as sequential executing instances with their own state.

quiz.question: Why do processes appear to have their own “virtual CPU”?
options: Because each process has its own physical core
Because the OS rapidly switches the real CPU among processes
Because the program counter is shared across processes
Because interrupts disable the scheduler
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Fast context switching creates the illusion that each process has its own CPU.

quiz.question: What is the process table used for?
options: To store only file system metadata
To store per-process information like registers, stack pointer, and resource usage
To map cache lines to memory addresses
To store only user interface commands
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The slides describe a process table entry containing vital per-process state and resources.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes threads, based on Week 1 Lesson 2?
options: Threads are separate processes with separate address spaces
Threads are execution entities scheduled by the CPU that share a process address space
Threads can only run in kernel mode
Threads eliminate the need for synchronization
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Threads share an address space inside a process and are scheduled execution units.

quiz.question: When do threads typically provide the biggest performance benefit?
options: When all work is purely CPU-bound
When the workload mixes substantial computation with I/O so activities can overlap
When the OS forbids interrupts
When there is only one process in memory
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The slides explain threads help most when computation and I/O overlap.

quiz.question: Which is a key per-thread resource mentioned in the slides?
options: Separate global variables
Separate stack for local variables and return addresses
Separate address space
Separate file system per thread
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Each thread has its own stack even though threads share the process address space.

quiz.question: What is an advantage of user-level threads compared to kernel threads?
options: Thread switching can avoid trapping into the kernel, making it fast
Page faults in one thread never affect other threads
Signals are always delivered to specific threads automatically
Forking multithreaded processes becomes simpler
quiz.explanation: Correct because: User-level thread management avoids kernel traps and can be faster.

quiz.question: What is a major drawback of user-level threads listed in Week 1 Lesson 2?
options: A page fault in one thread can block the whole process
Thread switching always requires a system call
User-level threads cannot share memory
User-level threads are slower than kernel threads
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The slides state a page fault on one user-level thread can block the entire process.

quiz.question: Which statement is true about kernel threads in Week 1 Lesson 2?
options: Kernel threads are tracked only in user space
Kernel thread creation and destruction are implemented as system calls
Kernel threads have no scheduling overhead
Kernel threads cannot handle page faults
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Kernel threads are managed by the OS and created/destroyed via system calls.

quiz.question: In the materials, what best distinguishes a type 1 hypervisor from a type 2 hypervisor?
options: Type 1 relies on a host OS; type 2 runs on bare hardware
Type 1 runs on bare hardware; type 2 uses a host OS for services like files and processes
Type 1 can only run Linux; type 2 can only run Windows
Type 1 is a container engine; type 2 is a process scheduler
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Type 1 is on bare metal, while type 2 leverages a host operating system for support.

quiz.question: How do containers differ from virtual machines in the Week 1 concept slide?
options: Containers always include a full guest OS per application
Containers share the host operating system and package apps with libraries
Containers require a type 1 hypervisor to run
Containers are slower because they emulate hardware
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Containers share the host OS and bundle app + dependencies, unlike VMs with full guest OSs.
